stances.claim: The CBCP is watching the long shadow cast by Obergefell v. Hodges because PH's three Constitutions carry due process and equal protection clauses in almost identical words to the 14th Amendment basis for the ruling

The Obergefell majority held that denying marriage licenses to same-sex couples is equivalent to a denial of the right to liberty under the due process clause and discrimination based on sex under the equal protection clause -- akin to denying school entry based on a student's Black color

The four dissenters used scathing language: Roberts accused the majority of judicial legislation ('Five lawyers have closed the debate'); Scalia called it 'hubris' and 'profoundly incoherent'; Thomas warned of religious-liberty threat ('liberty as freedom from government action, not entitlement to benefits'); Alito decried it as usurping the constitutional right of the people

The conservative wing (Roberts/Scalia/Thomas/Alito) believes in original intent of framers, judicial restraint, and state-over-federal primacy; the liberal wing (Breyer/Ginsburg/Sotomayor/Kagan) believes the Constitution should solve current problems and can invent new concepts like Miranda rights, right to abortion, and right against racial segregation

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes for the CBCP's semestral three-day meeting (July 11-12-13), which will discuss both current events and Pope Francis' recent encyclical Laudato Si. On current events, the bishops will look at the long shadow cast by the US Supreme Court's decision in Obergefell v. Hodges (June 26, 2015) -- passed 5-4 and penned by Justice Anthony Kennedy -- compelling all 50 US states to issue marriage licenses to same-sex couples 'on the same terms and conditions as marriages between persons of the opposite sex.' The majority held that denying marriage licenses to same-sex couples while granting them to opposite-sex couples constitutes a denial of the right to liberty under the due process clause and discrimination based on sex under the equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment -- akin to denying school entry to a student because of Black color. The four dissenters employed scathing words. CJ Roberts accused the majority of judicial legislation: 'Five lawyers have closed the debate and enacted their own vision of marriage... Those who founded our country would not recognize the majority's conception of the judicial role.' Scalia charged the majority with 'hubris,' its decision 'couched in a style that is as pretentious as its content is egoistic' with 'profundities [that] are often profoundly incoherent.' Thomas argued that 'liberty has been understood as freedom from government action, not entitlement to government benefits' and warned the decision threatens religious liberty. Alito decried it as usurping 'the constitutional right of the people to decide whether to keep or alter the traditional understanding of marriage.' To fully comprehend these acidic exchanges, the conservative wing -- Roberts/Scalia/Thomas/Alito -- believes the US Constitution should be interpreted in accordance with the original intent of the framers, that the Court should exercise judicial restraint and defer to elected officials, and that state governments should prevail over the federal. The liberal wing -- Breyer/Ginsburg/Sotomayor/Kagan -- believes the Charter should be interpreted to solve current problems, which may require inventing new concepts like Miranda rights, the right to abortion, and the right against racial segregation. Kennedy holds the swing vote; typically, as in Obergefell, he tilts the balance -- this is why the US Supreme Court is often referred to as the 'Kennedy Court' rather than the 'Roberts Court.' The CBCP is watching the long shadow because: (1) PH's 1935, 1973, and 1987 Constitutions carry due process and equal protection clauses in almost identical words; (2) a petition anchored on these clauses had already been filed in our SC on May 18, 2015 -- even before Obergefell -- to nullify portions of the Family Code defining marriage between a man and a woman; (3) after Obergefell, a congressman announced a bill legalizing same-sex marriage. CJ predicts the bishops, Catholic and other religious groups, and concerned citizens will fight this petition and bill as passionately as they did the Reproductive Health Law.
